title: Emor: appointed times (Leviticus 23)
hookLine: Shabbat, Passover, the Omer, Shavuot, the new year, Yom Kippur, Sukkot, all in one chapter

cards: Open a Jewish calendar and you'll see two systems at once. The ordinary months, January, February.
And, printed smaller, Hebrew months with names like Nisan and Tishrei, and holidays that wander across the ordinary calendar from year to year.
Ask where that second calendar comes from, and much of the answer is one chapter. Leviticus 23 lays out the sacred year from beginning to end, in forty-four verses.
The great festivals a Jewish family keeps today have their roots here; Hanukkah and Purim came later.

teach.b: The chapter opens, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "The appointed seasons of the LORD, which ye shall proclaim to be holy convocations". In Hebrew, mo'adim. A mo'ed is a set time, an appointment.
The Tent of Meeting, where God meets Moses, is the ohel mo'ed: same root. A holiday, in this picture, is a date God keeps with the people. Then the list.
Shabbat comes first, every seventh day. Then Passover and the week of matzah in spring. The first sheaf of barley, the omer, and seven weeks counted to Shavuot.
Then the seventh month: a day of blowing the horn, which became Rosh Hashanah; Yom Kippur on the tenth; and Sukkot, the festival of booths, on the fifteenth.
The verse says these are the times ye shall proclaim.
The Talmud tells of a dispute over when a month began, and reads the word for them, otam, as if it said atem, you: the people's court fixes the calendar, even if it errs.
God's appointments, the rabbis taught, are kept on the people's calendar.

And the year in Leviticus 23 isn't a list of days off. Spring is freedom, early summer is gift, fall is judgment, forgiveness and joy. It gives time a shape, so a year isn't one long run of the same day.

how: The Jewish calendar follows Leviticus 23's festivals on a lunar-solar year fixed by rabbinic calculation; Leviticus 22–23 is read in synagogue on several festivals, and some Jewish homes keep a Hebrew calendar beside the ordinary one.

games.q: a court proclaims a new month, and someone argues the date was wrong. whose date counts, in the Talmud's reading?
games.why: the times ye shall proclaim: the Talmud reads it as you, even if you err. the people keep God's appointments on their own calendar.

practice: Think about your year: which days stand out, and which blur together?
Bring to mind the next holiday that matters to you, a Jewish festival, a family day, an anniversary, and picture one thing that would keep the appointment: a meal, a call, a candle, a walk.
